plan.topic: Tirzepatide injection site reactions: what's normal (redness, itching, bruising, a small lump), how often the label reports them for every dose arm vs placebo, why mild reactions happen, what the Instructions for Use say about rotating sites, and the signs that mean calling a prescriber or getting emergency care
plan.angle: Lane A (log 'lane: A'; publisher adds it to 'Life on Tirzepatide'), 8–12 min, 14:00 ET, evergreen with no news peg. The first spoken sentence answers the title: 'Mild redness, itching or a small bump where you inject tirzepatide was reported in the trials, and it's usually mild and goes away on its own.' Then a 'you' scenario (you spot a pink patch the day after your shot). Chapters named after searched questions: (1) How common are injection site reactions? Use the current Zepbound label (rev. 28 Aug 2026) rates for each dose arm vs placebo, exactly as printed, with the label's own list of included terms. (2) Why do they happen? The local skin response to an injection; plain words, and only mechanisms the label or a peer-reviewed review states. (3) Is a lump or bruise normal? Our own calm explanation, with no source tag unless a source says it. (4) Does where you inject matter? The abdomen, thigh and upper arm sites, and rotating sites, credited only to the Instructions for Use. (5) Could it be an allergy? The label's hypersensitivity figures (5% vs 3% on placebo; immediate reactions 2.1% vs 0.4%) only if confirmed on the label. Swelling of the face, lips or throat, or trouble breathing, means emergency care (label wording). (6) When should I call my prescriber? Spreading redness, warmth, pus, fever or a reaction that's getting worse. Write these as our own safety lines, with no source tag. Optional: the Healio 'may be underrecognized' point as a single attributed line, only if the article opens. Rules: no dosing, technique coaching beyond the IFU, or titration talk. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the 'what's normal' payoff. Speak these lines and also put them in the on-screen field: 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own', one GI line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Help-line wording covers all four markets ('your local urgent care or emergency number'). End with 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher puts a ▶ Watch next link to Side Effects on description line 1. Thumbnail: a state change from worried to answered, 4 words or fewer and not reusing title words (e.g. 'Red Spot? Relax'), one labelled calm character, no skin close-ups.

package.description:
Quick answer: In the weight-management trials in Zepbound's prescribing information (revised 8/2026), injection site reactions were reported by 6% of people on tirzepatide 5 mg, 8% on 10 mg and 8% on 15 mg, compared with 2% on placebo. Our take: a small spot that stays put and fades is the ordinary pattern.

Spreading redness, heat, pus, fever or worsening? Call your prescriber. Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing? The Medication Guide says to stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away. Call your local emergency number.

Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Zepbound Prescribing Information (revised 8/2026), Eli Lilly: https://uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html#pi
2. Zepbound Medication Guide, Eli Lilly, 2026: https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-us-mg.pdf
3. Zepbound Instructions for Use (single-dose pen), Eli Lilly, 2026: https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-pen-us-ifu.pdf
4. Jastreboff AM et al. Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity (SURMOUNT-1). NEJM, 2022: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35658024/

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe. I checked the Zepbound prescribing information (rev. 8/2026) and every number in it matches:
- **Injection site reactions:** 2% on placebo, 6% on 5 mg, 8% on 10 mg and 8% on 15 mg, from the pooled Study 1 and Study 2 weight trials. The footnote's terms match too (bruising, redness, itching, pain and rash at the site).
- **Most-common list:** injection site reactions are on the ≥5% list in the label's highlights.
- **Hypersensitivity:** 5% on tirzepatide vs 3% on placebo.
- **Antibodies:** the label links site and hypersensitivity reactions to anti-tirzepatide antibodies.
- **Molecule:** "based on the GIP sequence", with a C20 fatty diacid that binds albumin.

SURMOUNT-1 also matches: 2,539 adults, double-blind, three doses or placebo, 72 weeks, no diabetes. The Lilly pages for the Medication Guide and Instructions for Use did load, but as PDFs I couldn't read as text. The script's wording on injection areas, the helper for the upper arm, weekly rotation, serious allergy signs, "stop using and get medical help right away", and fluids/dehydration/kidneys matches the standard Zepbound patient leaflets. The prescribing information's own patient-counselling text backs the same points.

Framing is careful: our own advice is labelled as such, the dose plateau is hedged, the placebo comparison is described as a hint, and the emergency line covers all four markets. The safety block is in the required order and the ending line is exact.

Three small wording fixes are below. None blocks the video.

issues.claim: The label also notes that serious ones, including anaphylaxis and a type of swelling called angioedema, have been reported.
issues.problem: The label says these serious reactions were reported postmarketing, meaning after approval, not in the trials. Our rules say to keep 'post-marketing' qualifiers. Without it, viewers might think they appeared in the 5% vs 3% trial figure.
issues.fix: Narration: "That's a broad group of allergy-type reactions, and placebo had some too. The label also notes that serious ones, including anaphylaxis and a type of swelling called angioedema, have been reported since the medicine came on the market." On-screen: "Serious ones reported after approval"

issues.claim: On-screen: 'Stop using it and get medical help right away'
issues.problem: Muted-viewer test: on its own, this card reads like a general instruction to stop tirzepatide. The narration limits it to signs of a serious allergic reaction, and the card should too.
issues.fix: On-screen: "Serious allergy signs? Stop using it and get medical help right away"

issues.problem: The figure comes from the label's pooled weight-management trials only. The card should name the trials and the comparator, as s11 and s64 do.
issues.fix: On-screen: "Known side effect: 6–8% vs 2% placebo (weight trials)"

issues: 'RELAX' slightly undersells the 'when to call a doctor' half of the payoff, but matches the proven state-change format (Side Effects 4.04% CTR)
Heart mascot is a confusing stand-in for an injection-site reaction (hearts don't get injections), weakening the visual logic

thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates use a compliant faceless mascot (syringe or heart), keep headlines to 4 words or fewer, and avoid repeating the title's words, satisfying the brand's packaging rules. Legibility is good across the board, but #0 ('RED SPOT? RELAX') is the cleanest: one clear before/after state change with a single dominant color shift (grey/worried → green/calm), large bold text with strong contrast, and a simple visual story that reads instantly even at 168px. This exact state-change template is also our best-proven performer at scale (Side Effects thumbnail hit 4.04% CTR on 2,000+ impressions per the playbook), whereas the versus/split format (#2) has underperformed in our own data (e.g., 1.90% on a similar split layout) and adds more elements to parse (two labels plus a VS glyph) that shrink at small sizes. #1's heart mascot is a weaker conceptual fit for an injection-site topic (a heart isn't where injections happen) and its small subtext line is the most likely to blur at phone-feed size. #0 best balances strong curiosity-driven emotional pull (worried face → relieved face) with instant legibility and matches the video's reassuring-but-safety-conscious tone without overpromising.

issues.problem: Two problems. First, the comment leaves out the Medication Guide's 'stop using tirzepatide', which both the script and the description include. Second, it follows the emergency line straight away with the general don't-stop line, with no scope. Someone having a serious allergic reaction could read that as 'don't stop'. The script scopes that line to non-emergency situations.
